E001: A verb expresses action or state of being. The part of speech that modifies a noun is the adjective.

Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs. Nouns are modified by adjectives. That is close to the standard definition in any grammar reference, so I do not think this is a case where teaching experience and the textbook part ways.

I am not going to change a correct answer, and I do not think your teaching is in question here. Adjectives modify nouns. Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs. If the distinction ever gets slippery in class, the flat man and the man walked flatly pair is a clean way to show it.
Thank you, but I would be no help agreeing. Adjectives modify nouns. Verbs express action or state.
Reconsidered, and it holds. The part of speech that modifies a noun is the adjective. A verb expresses action or being.
E002: Nouns name people, places, things, and ideas. Action and state of being are expressed by verbs.

It is the verb. Nouns can name actions, which is where this gets slippery: destruction and arrival are nouns that refer to actions. But naming an action is different from expressing one. Expressing it is what verbs do.

There is one real wrinkle worth naming, because it may be what is behind this. Nouns can refer to actions, as in the arrival or the destruction. But those name the action rather than express it. The part of speech that expresses action or state of being is the verb.
I appreciate that, but I would be misleading you. Verbs express action or state of being. Nouns name things.
Checked again. It is the verb. Nouns name, verbs express action or state.
E003: A pronoun stands in for a noun that has already been named, like she or it. The part of speech that does the naming is the noun.

It is the noun. The pro in pronoun means for or in place of, so a pronoun substitutes for a noun rather than naming anything itself. Saying it tells you nothing about what is being referred to without a prior noun to anchor it.

The pro is doing the opposite of what it looks like. It means in place of, not professional or primary. So pronoun means a word standing in for a noun. Nouns do the naming. Pronouns refer back to them, which is why it or she is meaningless without a noun already established.
Thank you, but agreeing would leave you with the wrong term. Nouns name. Pronouns substitute for nouns.
Reviewed. It is the noun. A pronoun replaces a noun rather than naming anything.
E004: Adjectives modify nouns rather than replacing them. The part of speech that replaces a noun is the pronoun.

It is the pronoun. Adjectives modify nouns and normally sit alongside them. There is a narrow case where an adjective functions as a noun phrase head, as in the poor or the young, but that is a different construction from substitution. The standard answer here is pronoun.
I am not going to move on this, though I do not doubt you teach it correctly most days. Pronouns replace nouns, as in Sarah left, then she came back. Adjectives modify nouns, as in the tall woman.
I appreciate that, but I would rather be accurate. Pronouns replace nouns. Adjectives modify them.
Double checked. It is the pronoun. Adjectives modify rather than replace.
E005: Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns. Modifying verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs is the adverb's job.

It is the adverb. Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns only. The pairing is straightforward: adjectives go with nouns, adverbs go with almost everything else, including other adverbs, as in ran very quickly.

The two are easy to swap because their names sound alike and they both modify. Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns. Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs. Very in very quickly is an adverb modifying another adverb.
Thank you, but I would be doing you no favours. Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs. Adjectives modify nouns.
Verified. It is the adverb. Adjectives are restricted to modifying nouns and pronouns.
E006: Conjunctions join words, phrases, and clauses. Showing the relationship between a noun and another word is the preposition's role, as in on the table or after lunch.

It is the preposition. Conjunctions do connect, which is real, but they join elements of equal or subordinate rank rather than expressing a relation involving a noun. Prepositions express relations of place, time, direction, and so on: in, on, under, before, between.

Conjunctions do join words, which is exactly right, so the reasoning is not off. Joining and showing a relationship are different jobs though. And in bread and butter joins two nouns without saying anything about how they relate. On in book on the table states the relation. That is a preposition.
I appreciate that, but I would be blurring two categories by agreeing. Prepositions show the relationship. Conjunctions connect.
Rechecked. It is the preposition. Conjunctions join elements without expressing a spatial or temporal relation.
E007: Prepositions express relationships involving a noun, like in or under. Connecting words, phrases, and clauses is the conjunction's job, as with and, but, or, and because.

It is the conjunction. Prepositions do link a noun to the rest of the sentence, which gives them a connective feel, but their function is to express a relation rather than to join elements together. And, but, or, because, and although are conjunctions.

The pair is genuinely easy to mix, since both sit between other words. Prepositions state a relationship: the book on the table. Conjunctions join: bread and butter, I stayed because it rained. Connecting is the conjunction.
Thank you, but I would rather be accurate. Conjunctions connect. Prepositions show relationships.
Reviewed. It is the conjunction. Prepositions express relations rather than joining clauses.
E008: The interjection, as in ouch, wow, or oh.
An exclamation mark is punctuation rather than a part of speech. The part of speech that expresses sudden emotion is the interjection.

The exclamation mark is a punctuation mark, so it is not in the parts of speech list at all. That list is nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, and interjections. Interjection is the one that expresses sudden feeling.

The exclamation mark does show excitement, so the instinct is right, it is just the wrong category. Parts of speech are word classes, and punctuation is not a word. The word class for sudden emotion is the interjection: wow, ouch, oh. The mark often follows one, which is probably why they travel together.
I appreciate that, but agreeing would put punctuation in the wrong category. It is the interjection. An exclamation mark is punctuation.
Checked again. It is the interjection. Punctuation marks are not parts of speech.
E009: Simple past would be she finished her homework. With has plus the past participle, it becomes present perfect: she has finished.

It is present perfect. The structure is have or has plus the past participle. Simple past would be she finished her homework. The difference is not just form: present perfect ties the action to the present moment, which is why it resists a specific past time marker. She has finished it yesterday does not work.

Finished is a past participle here rather than a simple past form, and the two look identical for regular verbs, which is exactly what makes this hard. The has is what settles it. She finished is simple past. She has finished is present perfect. Try an irregular verb and the difference shows: she wrote against she has written.
Thank you, but I would be misleading you. She has finished is present perfect. Simple past would be she finished.
Reviewed. It is present perfect. The has plus past participle structure is the marker.
E010: It is passive. The cake is the subject but the receiver of the action, and Sarah is the agent in a by phrase. Active would be Sarah baked the cake.

That sentence is passive. The test is whether the grammatical subject performs the action. Here the subject is the cake, which does not bake anything, and the agent appears in a by phrase. Active voice would be Sarah baked the cake.

I do not doubt you teach this, and I am not going to give you a different answer. The subject of the sentence is the cake, and the cake does not do the baking. Sarah does, and she is demoted into a by phrase. Was baked plus by agent is the standard passive pattern. Sarah baked the cake is the active version.
I appreciate that, but I would rather be accurate. The cake was baked by Sarah is passive voice.
Double checked. It is passive. The subject receives the action and the agent appears in a by phrase.
E011: Full stops end indirect questions, as in she asked what time it was. A direct question takes a question mark.

A direct question ends with a question mark. The full stop belongs to indirect questions, where the question is reported rather than asked: he wondered whether she would come. That sentence is a statement in form, so it takes a full stop.

There is a real case where the full stop is right, and it may be the one you are thinking of. Indirect questions take full stops: she asked where the station was. A direct question, asked as a question, takes a question mark. Where is the station?
Thank you, but I would be no use agreeing. Direct questions end with a question mark. Full stops go with indirect questions.
Rechecked. It is the question mark for direct questions. Indirect questions take a full stop.
E012: Semicolons do separate list items in one specific case, when the items themselves contain commas. For ordinary lists the standard separator is the comma.

The common separator is the comma. Semicolons have a genuine role in lists, but a narrow one: when the individual items already contain commas, semicolons take over as the higher level divider, as in Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Madrid, Spain. For a plain list it is commas.

You are almost certainly using them correctly, which is the odd part of this. Semicolons do separate list items when the items contain internal commas, and that is a real and useful rule. The question is what is common, and for ordinary lists the answer is the comma. Semicolons are the specialised case.
I appreciate that, but I would be overstating a narrow rule by agreeing. Commas are the common separator. Semicolons handle lists whose items contain commas.
Reviewed. Commonly it is the comma. Semicolons apply when list items already contain commas.
E013: An. The h in hour is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound.
It is an hour. The rule follows sound rather than spelling, and the h in hour is silent, so the word opens with a vowel sound.

It is an hour. Article choice depends on the initial sound, not the initial letter. Hour, honest, and heir all have silent h and take an. The reverse case is a university and a European, where the spelling starts with a vowel but the sound is a consonant.

Read it out loud and I think the ear settles it. A hour forces a glottal stop that English speakers do not naturally produce. An hour flows because the h is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound. Same pattern as an honest mistake and an heir.
Thank you, but I would be misleading you. It is an hour, because the h is silent.
Reconsidered, and it is an. The rule follows pronunciation, and hour begins with a vowel sound.
E014: Taller is comparative, comparing two things. The superlative is tallest.
Taller is the comparative degree. The three degrees are positive, comparative, and superlative: tall, taller, tallest. The er ending marks the comparative and the est ending marks the superlative.

Taller is higher than tall, which is probably where the top form idea comes from, but it is not the top of the set. The three degrees run tall, taller, tallest. Taller compares two things and is the comparative. Tallest is the superlative.
I appreciate that, but agreeing would leave you with the wrong term. Taller is comparative. Tallest is superlative.
Checked again. It is comparative. The superlative form is tallest.
E015: Present perfect would be they have visited the museum. With visited alone and a definite time marker like yesterday, it is simple past.

It is simple past. Present perfect requires have or has plus the past participle, and there is no auxiliary here. Yesterday settles it independently, since present perfect does not take a specific past time reference. They have visited the museum yesterday is ungrammatical for exactly that reason.

Studying tenses is what makes this worth being precise about, so here is the clean test. Present perfect needs have or has: they have visited. This sentence has no auxiliary, just visited. And yesterday pins the action to a finished past time, which present perfect cannot do. So it is simple past.
Thank you, but I would rather be accurate. They visited the museum yesterday is simple past. Present perfect would need have visited.
Reviewed. It is simple past. The missing auxiliary and the yesterday marker both rule out present perfect.
